newsitem.title: CONGO: Shots, explosions near Brazzaville presidency.
newsitem.headline: Shots, explosions near Brazzaville presidency.

text.p: Firefights intensified in the capital of Congo Brazzaville between the army and supporters of former president Denis Sassou Nguesso late on Friday, with witnesses reporting shots and explosions near the presidency.

Witnesses said shooting erupted near the presidency after the start of a second night of curfew in Brazzaville, where the government of Pascal Lissouba has ordered a crackdown on private militias and unauthorised possession of weapons.

One witness spoke of at least five rocket-propelled grenades or mortar shells exploding in or near the grounds of the presidency after a second day of clashes between the two sides. Lissouba's whereabouts were not immediately clear.
Witnesses earlier reported seeing a dozen corpses in the city centre. Some shops and businesses there had been looted.
The fighting broke out as the oil-producing former French colony prepared for presidential elections on July 27.

Sassou Nguesso, voted out of office in 1992 after the advent of multi-party politics, accuses Lissouba of seeking to foment violence with a view to postponing the election and has said his supporters will resist such action.
"There is no doubt they will resist. We cannot accept that the (electoral) process be put in doubt by force," he told Radio France International in an interview on Friday.
Political parties armed their supporters during ethnic and political fighting which killed 2,000 people after parliamentary elections in 1993.
The government later formally banned such private militias and the unauthorised carrying of arms.
Lissouba, Sassou Nguesso and Bernard Kolelas, the mayor of Brazzaville and 1992 runner-up, are likely to be the main candidates among about a dozen contesting the presidency.
Residents and visitors said national radio and television stopped broadcasting on Friday, while international telephone links were down.
Some contacts were possible via residents plugged into the mobile telephone network in Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of Congo across the Congo River.
Sassou Nguesso, a former military leader, ran a notionally Marxist single-party administration from 1979 until multi-party politics were introduced in the early 1990s.
The latest fighting followed clashes in the north of the country between his supporters and those of Lissouba's campaign manager in which at least 16 people were killed.

Officials say the army surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home on Thursday as part of efforts to arrest members of his entourage on murder charges stemming from the violence in the north. The suspects refused to surrender, they said.
Soldiers manned roadblocks in the centre of Brazzaville on Friday and restricted movements of vehicles. The road linking Maya-Maya international airport to the city centre was blocked.

France has economic interests in the Central African nation and its 350 troops there had been on standby to evacuate foreigners from Kinshasa in the last days of the civil war in former Zaire, now Kabila's Democratic Republic of Congo.
